strengths: Introduces a conceptually simple supervised SAE training scheme that enforces concept-to-latent assignments, directly targeting the feature-splitting problem in concept unlearning.
Reports strong UnlearnCanvas object-unlearning results: 91.51% average vs. 82.29% for SAeUron, with improvements in UA, IRA, and CRA, plus standard deviations over four seeds.

Demonstrates practical advantages beyond the main benchmark, including reduced inference-time multiplier search, improved sequential object unlearning, adversarial robustness evaluation, and NSFW suppression on I2P.
Provides useful qualitative and diagnostic analyses: score distributions, K-NN classification with the top-scoring latent, and visualizations of concept removal and patch attention.
Clearly situates the work in the SAE and diffusion-unlearning literature, with relevant background on TopK SAEs and prior unlearning methods.
weaknesses: The central one-to-one concept-latent claim is not rigorously validated. A single dominant score peak does not prove that other latents are inactive for the concept, and K-NN using the top latent being comparable to all features does not establish exclusivity. The main SAEMNESIA variant even matches SAeUron on the Cats-Dogs overlap analysis (10 overlapping timesteps), undercutting the claimed concept-separation improvement.

The comparison may be unfair: SAEMNESIA is reported with hyperparameter search, while several baselines appear to use default or originally reported settings. The authors recompute SAeUron due to an implementation inconsistency but do not re-evaluate all baselines under the same protocol, so the headline 9.22-point gain may partly reflect tuning asymmetry.

The adversarial-robustness section is internally inconsistent with the main results. The main table reports SAEMNESIA UA = 94.65 and SAeUron UA = 87.16, but the adversarial section states SAEMNESIA drops from 73.30% and the baseline from 26.19% to 2.22%, with no explanation of the different setting or metric.

The nudity-unlearning results contradict the single-latent erasure narrative: one-latent SAEMNESIA yields 47 detections versus SAeUron's 18, and only the two-latent TOP2 variant achieves 9 detections. This suggests the core single-latent intervention is brittle for real-world NSFW concepts.

The 96.67% hyperparameter-search reduction is based on an unjustified assumption that unsupervised search requires 30 latent combinations and 7 multipliers. It ignores training cost, score-function computation, and the need for labeled concept data, so the efficiency claim is overstated.

Reproducibility is limited. Key SAE and training details are missing or vague, including latent dimension/expansion factor, TopK k, number of training samples, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training steps, and compute resources. Code availability is not mentioned.

The sequential-unlearning claim of 28.4% improvement is shown only in a figure without numerical tables or variance, making it hard to assess reliability. Percentage language is also ambiguous: the 9.22% and 28.4% figures are absolute percentage-point differences, not relative improvements.

Limitations are not treated comprehensively. The method relies on concept labels derived from prompts, may not scale to arbitrary concepts, and fails on some blended object-style cases, but these constraints are not systematically discussed. Ethical discussion is limited to the positive safety use case without addressing dual-use or misuse risks.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: feature splitting in SAE-based concept unlearning is a real obstacle, and enforcing one-to-one concept-latent mappings via supervision is an intuitive, sensible remedy.

Strong headline result on the standard benchmark: 91.51% average on UnlearnCanvas object unlearning vs. 82.29% for SAeUron, with reported standard deviations across 4 seeds and consistent gains on UA/IRA/CRA.

The efficiency argument is practically relevant: if each concept truly maps to one latent, the inference-time search collapses from a multiplier x latent-combination grid to a single dimension, which is a meaningful usability improvement.

The paper reports a fairly broad empirical study (sequential unlearning over 9 objects, UnlearnDiffAtk adversarial robustness, I2P nudity removal) and a 10-variant ablation in the appendix that gives some insight into which design choices (CA loss, decorrelation, fine-tune vs. from-scratch) matter.

Using prompt structure to obtain concept labels 'for free' is a clean and low-cost supervision strategy, and the honesty about failure cases (e.g., flames/jellyfish blending with styles) in the appendix is appreciated.
weaknesses: The central thesis is undercut by the authors' own evidence. The paper claims one-to-one mapping enables erasure by steering a single latent, yet the default single-latent SAEMNESIA achieves 47 nudity detections on I2P versus SAeUron's 18 (Appendix 6.11); only the two-latent variant reaches 9. If the method requires two latents for nudity, the 'each concept is embedded in a single latent' claim is not generally true, and the abstract's assertion that SAEMNESIA 'effectively removes nudity when evaluated with I2P' is misleading, since the core method does substantially worse than the baseline.

The baseline comparison is ambiguous and potentially unfair. The text states an inconsistency was found in the public SAeUron implementation and that the authors 'recomputed the metrics ourselves using the corrected procedure,' yet Table 1 lists SAeUron at 82.29 (its original published number). It is unclear whether the baseline was re-evaluated under the same corrected procedure as SAEMNESIA; if not, the headline 9.22-point gap is not an apples-to-apples comparison. This is a reproducibility/soundness concern that is not resolved in the manuscript.

The validation of the core claim ('feature centralization') is weak. The k-NN experiment (Fig. 5) shows that a single top-scoring latent is sufficient for classification, but classification sufficiency does not demonstrate that all concept information is concentrated in that latent, nor that other latents are inactive. Likewise, the score histograms (Figs. 4, 10-12) show a dominant peak but do not establish that non-assigned latents are silent for the concept. No direct probing of what each latent responds to across diverse inputs is provided, so 'monosemanticity' is asserted rather than verified.

Limited originality relative to the stated contribution. Supervised SAEs and one-to-one dictionary assignments are not new, and the inference-time intervention (Eq. 10, a negative multiplier on a latent activation) is essentially the same mechanism used by SAeUron. The novelty is largely the application of supervision to an existing SAE-unlearning pipeline plus a specific loss combination (CA + DC), which is an incremental engineering step.

The '96.67% reduction in hyperparameter search' is a definitional comparison of search-space sizes (210 vs. 7 grid evaluations), not an empirical measurement of cost, and it depends on the authors' own chosen grid (7 multipliers x 30 latent combinations). It is presented as a headline efficiency result but carries little independent evidence.

Evaluation is narrow relative to the claims. All main results are on SD v1.5 (and v1.4 for I2P) with UnlearnCanvas; the 'architecture agnostic' claim is asserted but never demonstrated on another architecture or model family, and no cross-model transfer is shown.

Several reported improvements conflate percentage-point differences with relative percentages. '9.2% improvement' is 91.51 - 82.29 = 9.22 points, and '28.4% improvement' is 92.4 - 64.0 = 28.4 points (a ~44% relative gain). Presenting absolute differences as percentage improvements is imprecise and overstates the effect.

Reproducibility details are thin in places: the training data construction (80 prompts per object-style pair), the choice of 'block up.1.1', and the selective application of steering to the final 25 steps are somewhat ad hoc, and the metric-recomputation issue makes it hard for others to reproduce the comparison exactly.

strengths: Introduces a simple but novel supervised SAE framework that uses prompt-derived concept labels to enforce one-to-one concept-latent mappings, directly targeting feature splitting in SAE-based concept unlearning.
Reports strong quantitative results on the UnlearnCanvas object-unlearning benchmark: 91.51% average vs. 82.29% for SAeUron, with improved UA, IRA, and CRA (Table 1).

Demonstrates substantial inference-time efficiency: single-latent steering reduces hyperparameter search from 210 evaluations to 7, and learned multipliers are much smaller on average than SAeUron's (-6.60 vs. -21.25; Table 3).
Shows convincing sequential-unlearning scalability, achieving 92.4% UA for 9-object removal versus 64% for the baseline, while also improving retention accuracy.
Provides evidence of improved adversarial robustness under UnlearnDiffAtk, retaining 28.30% unlearning accuracy after attack versus 2.22% for the baseline.
Includes practical NSFW evaluation on I2P, where the two-latent variant achieves 9 NudeNet detections versus SAeUron's 18, with competitive CLIPScore and FID.
Supports interpretability claims with score-distribution plots, KNN classification using only the top-scoring latent, and patch-activation visualizations that show concentrated concept attention.
Related work is well covered, and the appendix provides useful standard deviations, ablations, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central 'feature centralization' claim is not fully proven: the concept-assignment loss only encourages the assigned latent to activate for present concepts and does not explicitly penalize other latents from encoding the same concept, so residual feature splitting may remain. KNN top-1 sufficiency does not demonstrate exclusivity; causal ablation of non-assigned latents and aggregate centralization metrics are needed.

The main SAEMNESIA variant does not improve the known Dogs-vs-Cats overlap problem: Table 8 shows OS-DC-CA-FT has 10 overlapping timesteps, the same as SAeUron, while other variants achieve zero overlap but are not the primary model.

There is an internal inconsistency in Table 5: OS-DC-CA-FT's components (UA 91.75, IRA 93.16, CRA 88.60) average to 91.17, not the reported 91.51; Table 1 reports different component values (94.65/91.39/88.48) for what appears to be the same SAEMNESIA variant, raising reproducibility concerns.

Reproducibility is incomplete: key SAE details such as expansion factor, latent dimension, TopK value, training epochs, optimizer, batch size, learning rate, and compute requirements are missing, and no code release is mentioned. The referenced appendix sections do not fully specify the architecture and training protocol.

The NSFW result relies on a two-latent variant, SAEMNESIA-TOP2, while the one-latent method performs worse than SAeUron (47 vs. 18 detections). The abstract and conclusion overstate 'effectively removes nudity' without foregrounding this exception, and the two-neuron variant conflicts with the one-to-one mapping premise for this case.

Generalization is limited: all experiments use SD v1.5 or v1.4 and one U-Net block (up.1.1) for object features. The claim of architecture agnosticism is not tested on SDXL, DiT, or other diffusion backbones.

The 96.67% search reduction is somewhat overstated because it depends on an assumed 30-latent-combination search for the unsupervised baseline; the proposed method still requires multiplier search per concept and is sensitive to the supervised loss weight, as beta=10 collapses generation to white images.

The main paper lacks an explicit limitations section, and broader limitations such as label dependence for new concepts, residual concept leakage, computational cost of SAE training, and evaluation scope are only partially discussed in the appendix.
Improvement claims are phrased ambiguously: the 9.22% and 28.4% figures are percentage-point gains, not relative improvements, which may mislead readers.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, well-motivated method: using concept labels derived directly from prompts to train a supervised TopK SAE that enforces one-to-one concept-latent mappings, which simplifies inference-time unlearning to steering a single latent.
Strong empirical results on the UnlearnCanvas object benchmark (91.51% avg vs. 82.29% for SAeUron), with consistent gains across UA (+7.49), IRA (+5.82), and CRA (+14.34).

The interpretability claim is supported by multiple converging analyses: score-distribution histograms showing a dominant peak (Fig. 4, Fig. 9), K-NN classification showing the top-1 latent matches all-latent performance (Fig. 5), and patch/timestep activation visualizations (Fig. 7).

Comprehensive evaluation beyond the main benchmark: sequential object unlearning (92.4% vs. 64% for 9 objects), white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) adversarial robustness, and NSFW suppression on I2P.

Ablations over loss variants (Tables 7-9) and a decorrelation constraint to separate object vs. style groups, with an honest discussion of limitations (closed vocabulary, within-group interference, scaling to large concept sets).

Good reproducibility: SAE architecture (TopK, k=32, expansion 16), optimizer settings, and loss hyperparameters (β, λ, η) are all reported, along with standard deviations over seeds and a computational-cost analysis.
weaknesses: The interpretability framing is somewhat circular: since the supervised loss explicitly forces assigned latents to activate for their concept, the resulting 'feature centralization' is largely by construction rather than a discovered property. The method sidesteps feature splitting with labels rather than solving it, which weakens the novelty relative to SAeUron.

The abstract overclaims on nudity suppression ('effectively suppresses nudity'), while the primary single-latent method achieves only 47 detections (worse than SAeUron's 18). Only the unmentioned TOP2 variant reaches 9, which contradicts the paper's central one-latent-per-concept narrative for the NSFW case.

On the core object-unlearning benchmark, SAEmnesia (91.51%) is not state of the art: SalUn reaches 94.28%. The method only wins on the combined object+style average, which somewhat limits the significance of the headline result.
Gains on style unlearning (98.19 vs. 98.10) and held-out concept generalization (73.75 vs. 72.32, Table 17) are marginal, suggesting the supervised mapping transfers weakly to unseen concepts.

The 96.67% hyperparameter-search reduction is an artifact of the design choice (one latent vs. m×l search) rather than an independent empirical result, and is presented somewhat as an achievement in itself.

The requirement for labeled concepts limits practical applicability to closed vocabularies; for NSFW the SAE was trained on only two prompts, which likely explains the weak centralization and the need for TOP2 steering.

Some minor presentation issues: inconsistent reference years (e.g., ESD cited as 2023 but listed as Gandikota et al., 2024; Cywiński & Deja labeled 2024 in one place and 2025 elsewhere) and several low-resolution figures.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper correctly identifies feature splitting as the bottleneck of unsupervised SAE-based unlearning and proposes an intuitive, transparent remedy (supervised concept-latent binding).

Consistent empirical gains on the main benchmark: on UnlearnCanvas object unlearning, SAEmnesia improves over SAeUron by +9.22 average points (91.51 vs 82.29) with gains on all three metrics (UA +7.49, IRA +5.82, CRA +14.34), and it also edges out SAeUron on combined object+style unlearning (94.85 vs 90.10, Table 15).

Practical efficiency arguments: single-latent steering collapses the multiplier×latent search (210→7 evaluations) and the measured inference overhead is even slightly lower than SAeUron (1.89% vs 2.56%, Table 4), which is a plausible practical benefit.

The robustness evaluation is a genuine plus: both a white-box gradient attack (UnlearnDiffAtk) and a black-box attack (Ring-A-Bell) are run, with SAEmnesia retaining 57.5% and 97% UA respectively versus 34.2% and 79.5% for SAeUron (Table 2).
Sequential unlearning scalability is convincingly demonstrated (92.4% vs 64% UA for 9-object removal, Fig. 8), which is the setting where one-to-one mappings should help most.
The paper is honest about limitations (closed-vocabulary constraint, within-group interference, scalability, backbone coverage) and includes a thoughtful impact statement.
The appendix provides substantive ablations (from-scratch vs fine-tuned, global-CE vs CA loss, pre/post-TopK supervision, held-out concepts, per-object disentanglement).
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim (that SAEmnesia 'eliminates feature splitting' and achieves feature centralization) is supported by evidence that is partly circular. The CA loss (Eq. 8) explicitly maximizes the assigned latent's pre-activation for the target concept, so the dominant score peak in Fig. 4 is what the objective optimizes by construction; the paper never shows that the *other* latents that previously responded to the concept have been suppressed, which is what 'eliminating splitting' would actually require. The 2.43× peak-height comparison is therefore not strong evidence for the mechanistic claim, even if the downstream unlearning results are real.

Evaluation is narrow: a single backbone (SD v1.5), a single benchmark (UnlearnCanvas), and effectively a single SAE-family baseline (SAeUron). In Table 1, SalUn (94.28) actually outperforms SAEmnesia (91.51) on object unlearning, so the 'state-of-the-art' framing rests entirely on the SAE sub-family and on the combined metric.

The fairness and reproducibility of the headline comparison are unclear. The method is described as starting from 'a pretrained unsupervised SAE' and fine-tuning it, but it is not stated whether this is SAeUron's released checkpoint or a separately trained SAE. If it is a different SAE, the +9.22 comparison conflates the supervised loss with a different base representation. No code release is mentioned and training details (layer choice, data, seeds) are sparse.

The nudity results are presented in a way that overstates the method. The main text claims SOTA (9 detections vs SAeUron's 18), but Appendix A.14 shows this requires a different variant (SAEmnesia-TOP2, two latents, multiplier -600), while the base SAEmnesia achieves 47 detections — worse than SAeUron's 18. The main-text phrasing conflates these variants, and the -600 multiplier is extreme enough that the 'preserved quality' claim (only CLIPScore/FID reported) is not fully convincing.

Novelty is incremental over SAeUron: the core addition is a supervised CA loss plus a decorrelation term on top of an existing TopK SAE pipeline, with labels that are trivially available from prompts. The decorrelation contribution is marginal (91.51 with DC vs 89.82 without, Tables 8–9), so the main driver is the simple supervised activation-boosting loss.

The 96.67% hyperparameter-reduction figure is a contrived metric that assumes SAeUron must search 30 latent combinations (7×30=210); the actual search complexity of the baseline is not established, so the headline efficiency number is a strawman rather than a measured quantity.

Backbone-generalization evidence is weak: in Table 12 (SDXL-Turbo) IRA collapses to 45.15 and CRA is omitted, with the shortfall attributed to a domain gap in the evaluation protocol — which means the architecture-agnostic claim is essentially unsupported.
Held-out concept generalization is marginal (73.75 vs 72.32, Table 17, a ~1.4-point gain), which weakens the claim that the supervised mapping 'transfers' rather than overfits.

Several central claims are asserted rather than demonstrated: the causal link from 'higher score peak' to 'more robust erasure' (Section 4.2, A.5) is stated as a hypothesis, and the claim that gains stem from stronger concept-latent associations is not isolated from confounds such as fine-tuning on the benchmark's own prompts.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated supervised SAE training scheme that explicitly enforces concept-latent assignments during training, directly targeting the feature-splitting problem that makes unsupervised SAE-based unlearning expensive and imprecise.

Delivers strong, consistent empirical gains on the UnlearnCanvas object benchmark (91.51% avg, +9.22 points over SAeUron) across all three metrics (UA +7.49, IRA +5.82, CRA +14.34), which is a meaningful advance over the SAE-based state of the art.

The single-latent intervention substantially reduces inference-time tuning (reported 96.67% reduction in hyperparameter search), and the inference overhead (1.89%) is even lower than the SAeUron baseline, making the method practically attractive.

Sequential unlearning scalability is compelling: 92.4% vs 64% accuracy for 9-object removal, and higher retention accuracy when all objects are erased, supporting the claim that interpretable, specialized neurons reduce interference during cumulative edits.

Feature centralization is supported by multiple complementary analyses: score-distribution peaks (Figure 4, 2.43x improvement), K-NN classification showing top-1 latent matches all-features accuracy (Figure 5), and spatially/temporally coherent activation patterns (Figure 7).
Robustness claims are tested against two distinct threat models (white-box UnlearnDiffAtk and black-box Ring-A-Bell), with a clear advantage over SAeUron in both clean and attacked conditions.
Reproducibility is well handled: full SAE/loss hyperparameters, standard deviations over 4 seeds, training-time breakdowns, and use of the baseline's public checkpoints/code.
The limitations section is candid and identifies concrete failure modes (closed vocabulary, within-group interference, scalability to open vocabularies), which is helpful for future work.
weaknesses: The paper's central 'feature centralization / one-to-one mapping' claim is only partially supported. The Dogs-vs-Cats overlap analysis (Table 11) shows the primary model (OS-DC-CA-FT) still has 10 overlapping timesteps—identical to the SAeUron baseline—so splitting and interference persist for semantically similar concepts, which directly undercuts the headline claim.

The abstract and Section 4.4 state that SAEmnesia 'effectively suppresses nudity' with '9 detections vs. SAeUron's 18,' but this is only achieved by the SAEmnesia-TOP2 variant that steers two latents with a multiplier of -600 (versus -49 for the single-latent version, which yields 47 detections). This contradicts the single-latent framing and should be presented as such in the main text, not buried in Appendix A.14.

Style unlearning gains are marginal (98.19 vs 98.10), and the paper's framing that style erasure is 'easier' is asserted rather than rigorously justified; a more balanced treatment would help substantiate the generality of the method.

Generalization beyond SD v1.5 is weak: on SDXL-Turbo, SAEmnesia reaches only 63.63% UA with IRA dropping to 45.15%, which is far from the strong results on SD v1.5 and raises questions about the method's architecture-agnostic claim.

The 96.67% efficiency claim rests on an assumed SAeUron search over 30 latent combinations, which is a heuristic assumption about the baseline's tuning procedure rather than a measured requirement; the reported reduction is therefore not fully grounded.

Since the supervision labels are derived directly from the same prompts/concepts the method aims to erase, the approach is essentially a targeted supervised fine-tuning of the SAE; the framing as a general interpretability tool should be tempered relative to the more limited scope of the demonstrated results.

Some ablation inconsistencies are not resolved in the main text (e.g., global-CE from-scratch underperforms while the fine-tuned variant is strong; OS-TK-CA-FT behaves very differently across Tables 8 and 9), which makes it harder to attribute gains cleanly to the proposed CA/DC losses.
